topic: The Mystery of Pi in the Normal Distribution

outline.topic: The Mystery of Pi in the Normal Distribution

sections.title: The Hook: Why does a Circle show up in Statistics?
sections.content: Introduce the standard normal distribution curve f(x) = C * e^(-x²/2). Pose the question: Why is the normalization constant C exactly 1/sqrt(2π)? Compare a bell-shaped curve with a geometry problem involving circles.
sections.example: Visualize a dartboard: Imagine throwing thousands of darts at a wall; the horizontal and vertical landing positions follow a bell curve. Why does the area under this curve involve the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Gaussian Integral
sections.content: Define the target integral I = ∫ e^(-x²) dx from -∞ to +∞. Explain that this function has no elementary antiderivative, making direct integration impossible via standard calculus methods.
sections.example: An animation showing an attempt to 'fill' the area under the curve using rectangles that fail to capture the smooth curvature.

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: Polar Coordinates
sections.content: Introduce the trick of squaring the integral: I² = (∫ e^(-x²) dx) * (∫ e^(-y²) dy). Convert this into a double integral over the entire 2D plane: ∫∫ e^-(x²+y²) dA. Explain the shift to polar coordinates where x²+y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ.
sections.example: Visual transition: A grid of square tiles (Cartesian) morphing into a circular target pattern (Polar). The constant 'r' emerges naturally from the Jacobian of the transformation.

sections.title: Solving the Integral
sections.content: Solve the polar integral: ∫[0, 2π] dθ * ∫[0, ∞] r * e^(-r²) dr. The 2π appears instantly from the dθ integration, providing the source of the π in the final result.
sections.example: Show an animation of a robot sweeping a circle with a radar beam, highlighting the '2π' rotation required to cover the area, which acts as the source of the hidden constant.

sections.title: Conclusion: Normalization
sections.content: Since I² = π, then I = sqrt(π). To ensure the total area under the probability density function equals 1, the constant 1/sqrt(2π) must be placed in front of the bell curve.
sections.example: Display the final normal distribution graph filling with water to exactly the '1.0' mark, showing that the 1/sqrt(2π) factor acts as the perfect 'scaling lid' for the distribution.
